items.text: Acute symptomatic seizure: occurs in close association with an acute insult, such as hypoglycaemia or stroke.
Unprovoked seizure: occurs without an immediate provoking insult.
Epilepsy: a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, meeting accepted diagnostic criteria.

blocks.text: Modern classification begins with the onset of the seizure.

items.text: Tonic-clonic seizure: stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking.
Absence seizure: brief episodes of impaired awareness, often with staring.
Myoclonic seizure: brief, sudden muscle jerks.
Atonic seizure: sudden loss of muscle tone.
Focal impaired-awareness seizure: impaired awareness with possible automatisms.

blocks.text: **Definition:** A seizure lasting at least 5 minutes, or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness between episodes.

items.text: **T** – Time the seizure and call for help.
**I** – Immediate ABC assessment; protect airway and provide oxygen if indicated.
**M** – Medication: give an appropriate benzodiazepine according to emergency protocol.
**E** – Escalate to second-line antiseizure treatment if the seizure persists; investigate and treat the underlying cause.

blocks.text: Important investigations include bedside glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal function, liver function, toxicology where appropriate and brain imaging when indicated.
**Exam pearl:** Do not delay treatment of convulsive status epilepticus while waiting for investigations. Check glucose promptly and correct hypoglycaemia.

blocks.text: Delirium is an acute disturbance in attention and awareness, usually with a fluctuating course.

items.text: Alzheimer's disease – most common cause; progressive memory impairment.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** In a patient with suspected dementia, assess potentially reversible contributors such as depression, hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, medication effects and chronic subdural haematoma.

blocks.text: 1.Ischaemic stroke – interruption of blood supply to brain tissue.
2.Haemorrhagic stroke – bleeding into or around the brain.
The five categories are conventionally listed as large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-vessel occlusion, other determined cause and undetermined cause.
Other important risk factors include older age, obesity, physical inactivity, carotid stenosis and previous TIA or stroke.
Other mimics include brain tumours and functional neurological disorders.

items.text: TIA: transient focal neurological dysfunction caused by cerebral, spinal or retinal ischaemia without acute infarction.
Stroke: neurological dysfunction due to acute brain, spinal cord or retinal infarction, or haemorrhage.

blocks.text: Suspected stroke requires urgent brain imaging. Non-contrast CT is commonly performed initially to exclude haemorrhage. A normal early CT does not exclude acute ischaemic stroke.

items.text: UMN: tone and reflexes generally go up.

blocks.text: **Important exception:** Acute UMN lesions may initially produce flaccidity and reduced reflexes (spinal shock). These findings can evolve into spasticity and hyperreflexia.

blocks.title: A systematic neurological examination should include:

items.text: **M – Mental status:** consciousness, orientation, memory, speech and higher functions.
**C – Cranial nerves:** assess all 12 cranial nerves.
**M – Motor system:** muscle bulk, tone, power and involuntary movements.
**S – Sensory system:** light touch, pain, temperature, vibration and proprioception.
**R – Reflexes:** deep tendon reflexes and plantar response.
**C – Coordination:** finger-nose, heel-shin and rapid alternating movements.
**G – Gait:** normal gait, tandem gait, heel walking and toe walking where safe.
